passages.section: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
passages.location: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
passages.text: Code-as-policy agents often use execution feedback to retry failed programs. Additional sampling and task guidance can also improve success, leaving the contribution of failure-specific feedback unclear. We study this question in simulated robot manipulation. A fixed lookup selects feedback templates using failure labels and the API variant. A frozen code model generates a fresh program after each scene reset. On the same 252 initial failures, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B recovers 85.3% within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The advantage persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance yield similar recovery point estimates, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to that of template-based feedback. Template-based feedback also lowers recovery on a nut-insertion task requiring a rim grasp, consistent with an incompatible center-grasp instruction. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, and concise, task-compatible static guidance as baselines.

passages.section: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
passages.location: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
passages.text: Keywords: Code-as-policy agents, Self-repair, Execution feedback, Test-time evaluation

Code-as-policy agents translate language instructions into executable robot programs [ 1 ] . Their failures often follow clear patterns: a program may skip the grasp, release an object after lifting, or place it away from the target. A common response is iterative self-reflection. The model reads its failed program and execution trace, writes a critique, and tries again [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Retry success can reflect additional sampling, concise task instructions, feedback about the current failure, or editing the previous program. We ask whether feedback after failure improves recovery over guidance available from the first attempt.

We study this question with frozen Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B models in a reset-and-retry setting. Each retry starts from the original scene. Our main conditions generate a fresh program with the failed program omitted from the prompt. We use template-based feedback to study which information improves retry success. A fixed lookup selects instructions using the failure label and API variant, such as “MUST grasp the object before lifting.” We call this condition Compiled . The lookup lets us replace matched feedback with another episode’s feedback, hold the guidance fixed, or remove it while keeping the retry loop unchanged (Figure 1 ). Separate editing conditions expose the previous program and request a revision. All conditions restart the original scene. We do not test recovery from the physical state left by failure.

Figure 1: Template-based feedback improves recovery over resampling. (a) Reset-and-retry loop and feedback methods. (b) Recovery on 252 initial failures, with similar outcomes for Compiled, Different-Label Feedback, and Fixed Task Template.

Compiled recovers 85.3% of the 252 initial failures within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The gain persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and one fixed template per task produce similar point estimates. We detect no benefit from matching the coarse failure label to the current episode. The confidence intervals still allow differences between conditions. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to Compiled’s, with fewer tokens per solved episode. That comparison changes initial guidance and the generation instruction together. Their individual contributions remain unresolved.

We compare feedback content and program-generation strategies under matched retry budgets to test how additional sampling, reusable task guidance, and failure-label matching affect recovery. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include static guidance as a baseline for adaptive feedback.

Language models for robot control. Code as Policies and ProgPrompt generate executable programs from grounded robot skills [ 1 , 5 ] . SayCan selects actions using language-model and affordance scores [ 6 ] . CaP-X evaluates code-generating agents across robot APIs and feedback modalities, including multi-turn interaction without scene resets [ 7 ] . Robot recovery systems often ask a model to interpret a failure. REFLECT summarizes robot experience to support failure explanation and correction [ 8 ] . DoReMi compares a plan with its execution [ 9 ] . TCoT adds trajectory-level reasoning to a vision-language-action model [ 10 ] . Our reset-based comparisons examine feedback content and program-generation strategies on paired episodes under matched retry budgets.

Evaluation of iterative self-repair. Reflexion and Self-Refine use model-written critiques to improve later outputs [ 2 , 3 ] . Self-Debugging conditions code generation on the previous program and its execution results [ 4 ] . On code benchmarks, Olausson et al. [11] found that self-repair often does not outperform independent sampling at matched compute. Self-correction of reasoning is also unreliable without external feedback, whereas critique grounded in external evidence can help [ 12 , 13 ] . We extend matched-sampling comparisons to embodied code execution and test whether guidance must match the current failure or follow a failure at all.

Execution feedback and interactive evaluation. CodeRL, RLEF, and MURPHY use compiler or test feedback to update model parameters [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] . RLEF also tests random execution feedback from unrelated programming problems at inference time. This comparison tests the value of feedback specific to the current problem, although its training, tasks, and feedback construction differ from ours. Inference-time agents such as ReAct, Voyager, and LATS use feedback during search or interaction [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] . InterCode, AppWorld, and AgentBoard evaluate execution outcomes and intermediate progress [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . With model weights fixed, we ask which information in a robot’s retry prompt accounts for recovery.

We evaluate frozen code models in robosuite simulation with a Panda arm [ 23 , 24 ] . Models receive state information and generate Python programs using a documented robot API, without images. The primary evaluation uses Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct [ 25 ] with the primitive API on cube lifting and stacking.

An episode comprises an initial program execution for a task and scene, followed by any retries under one method. The initial execution is attempt 0 . After an initial failure, the model is allowed up to five retries . Before each retry, the simulator resets to the original scene. Each retry produces a complete program, either generated from scratch or revised from the previous program.

We use 252 initial failures for evaluation and 40 for development. The sets contain distinct initial programs, identified by their hashes. The evaluation covers 159 combinations of task, API variant, and scene, including 24 also used in development. All methods are evaluated on the same stored initial failures. The end-to-end studies pair methods by scene seed.

Conditional recovery@ k k is the fraction of attempt-0 failures solved within k k retries. This metric measures sequential retries and differs from pass@ k k estimated from independent samples. For end-to-end studies, initial success is success on attempt 0 and overall success@6 is success in any of the six allowed executions. An attempt is valid if its program compiles, uses only documented API functions, and finishes before timeout.

The generalization study includes Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B and two additional pick-and-place tasks. We combine results across seven settings that meet the predefined eligibility criteria. Separate studies examine API variants with fewer high-level helper functions, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B [ 26 ] . Further details of the software, tasks, evaluation sets, and metrics are provided in Appendix A .

After an unsuccessful execution, a rule-based labeler assigns one primary label from a 14-label taxonomy. Compiled maps this label and the API variant to a fixed feedback template containing a diagnosis and short MUST/NEVER instructions (Table 1 ). This lookup requires no additional model call. The instructions guide code generation without imposing execution-time checks.

Compiled accumulates feedback from the initial failure and subsequent failed retries, retaining the labels and attempt indices. The feedback block presents the newest feedback first, omits duplicate instruction lines, and respects the feedback-length limit. The generation prompt contains the task, API documentation, and accumulated feedback, with the previous program omitted. An example from the earlier study shows an initial failure followed by a successful fresh retry (Figure 2 a). The prompts are provided in Appendix B , and the reset-and-retry algorithm is given in Algorithm 1 .
Table 1: Failure labels select fixed retry guidance. Example instruction excerpts for the primitive API. Full templates are provided in Appendix D .

Detected failure Guidance added to the retry prompt Grasp did not secure the object MUST: grasp at the object’s CENTRE: …, with the gripper empty Object grasped but not lifted MUST: … call lift(name, height=0.1) after the grasp Unsupported function call MUST: use ONLY the documented API functions … NEVER: import statements

We compare methods within each study using the same generator, task, API, decoding settings, and retry limit. Resample repeats the base retry prompt without feedback. Other-Episode Feedback replaces the current episode’s feedback with feedback from other failures, matched by task, API variant, and initial task-progress bin. The primary matching control, Different-Label Feedback , selects individual feedback records from other episodes of the same task, preferring the same initial task-progress bin and requiring a different failure label whenever available. Both add feedback as the evaluated episode accumulates failures and use the same feedback-length limit. These controls test the value of matching the coarse failure label while retaining useful task information. The matching and fallback rules are specified in Appendix B.3 .

We select a fixed template for each task from the development data, choosing the most frequent failure label with task-compatible guidance. Fixed Task Template reuses this template across retries after the initial failure. Static-from-Start uses the complete Fixed Task Template retry prompt from attempt 0, changing both the initial generation instruction and the presence of guidance.

Direct+Compiled shows the failed program and requests an edit, jointly changing code exposure and the generation instruction. Reflection uses an extra model call to critique the failed program and execution log. Its generation call receives the accumulated critiques and omits the previous code. Reflection was tested only in the earlier core evaluation with the original generation instruction.

The primary evaluation uses a condition-neutral generation instruction for regeneration methods. The original instruction referred to a repair plan even when feedback was absent. Both prompt versions are provided in Appendix B.4 .
Eligibility criteria, multiplicity corrections, decoding settings, and token accounting are specified in Appendix A .

Figure 2: Guidance improves recovery under fixed token budgets. (a) An initial failure followed by a successful retry after reset. (b) Recovery under total-token budgets. (c) Paired recovery@5 comparisons show an advantage over resampling, with no detected advantage over different-label or fixed-template guidance.

In the primary evaluation, Compiled recovers 85.3% of the 252 held-out failures within five retries. Resample, with the same retry cap, recovers 68.3%, a difference of + 17.1 +17.1 pp (95% CI [ + 9.9 , + 24.2 ] [+9.9,+24.2] ). 1 1 1 pp denotes percentage points. Bands and error bars show 95% CIs: Wilson for recovery proportions and paired bootstrap for differences. Compiled recovers more failures than Resample from the first retry (Figure 1 b) and uses fewer total model tokens, including prompts and completions.

Under fixed token budgets, Compiled improves recovery over Resample by + 15.9 +15.9 pp at 2,000 tokens and + 14.7 +14.7 pp at 5,000 (Figure 2 b). Fixed Task Template and Different-Label Feedback yield similar observed recovery rates to Compiled, while Direct+Compiled has lower recovery. Compiled also achieves higher overall success than Resample in the earlier 700-scene end-to-end study with the original generation instruction (Appendix C ).

Different-Label Feedback and Fixed Task Template each recover 86.1% in the primary evaluation, compared with 85.3% for Compiled. We detect no advantage from matching the coarse label to the current failure, although the paired confidence intervals do not establish equivalence (Table 2 ; Figure 2 c). In earlier studies, we also detected no advantage for Compiled over Other-Episode Feedback, Permuted Labels, or Initial-Label Only (Appendix C ).

In the primary evaluation, the exploratory Repeated API Rules control copies rules already in the prompt and does not reproduce Compiled’s improvement. Earlier comparisons using the original generation instruction likewise show lower recovery with content-free feedback and All-Template Union than with concise feedback templates (Appendix C ).
Table 2: Primary paired contrasts on 252 initial failures. Each entry is Compiled minus the comparator in recovery@5, with a 95% paired-bootstrap CI.

Comparator Question Δ \Delta (pp; 95% CI) Resample benefit beyond another sample? + 17.1 +17.1 [ + 9.9 , + 24.2 ] [+9.9,+24.2] Different-Label Feedback must the label match? − 0.8 -0.8 [ − 6.3 , + 4.8 ] [-6.3,+4.8] Fixed Task Template dynamic versus fixed guidance? − 0.8 -0.8 [ − 6.7 , + 5.2 ] [-6.7,+5.2] Direct+Compiled does editing improve recovery? + 63.9 +63.9 [ + 56.7 , + 70.6 ] [+56.7,+70.6]

On 700 new scenes, Static-from-Start increases initial success from 19.3% with the standard prompt to 36.9%. It uses the complete Fixed Task Template retry prompt from the first attempt, changing both task guidance and the generation instruction. Their individual contributions remain unresolved.

By the sixth execution, Static-from-Start reaches 92.4% overall success, compared with 89.6% for Compiled and 90.1% for Fixed Task Template (Figure 3 ). Its advantage over Compiled is not statistically significant after multiplicity correction ( + 2.9 +2.9 pp; Holm-adjusted p = 0.13 p{=}0.13 ). It also uses the fewest total model tokens per solved episode. Complete results and prompt differences are reported in Appendix C.2 .

Figure 3: A fixed guided prompt improves initial success. (a) Initial and overall success on 700 fresh scenes. (b) Total model tokens per solved episode. Static-from-Start changes both the initial instruction and guidance.
The matching controls and Static-from-Start results suggest that reusable task guidance accounts for the gain. These results do not establish that the model uses the current execution trace.

Direct+Compiled achieves 21.4% recovery in the primary evaluation. Earlier analyses show smaller program changes with editing than with fresh generation. Because Direct+Compiled changes code exposure and the generation instruction together, the cause of its lower recovery remains unresolved.

In the earlier core evaluation, Reflection achieves 56.0% recovery, below Resample, while using more completion tokens and wall-clock time. These findings concern the tested editing and reflection implementations. Further editing and critique results are summarized in Appendix C.1 .
Figure 4: Guidance benefits vary across tasks and models. Compiled–Resample recovery differences across evaluated settings. The diamond summarizes the seven eligible generalization settings.

Across seven Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B settings covering four tasks and 354 initial failures, Compiled improves recovery@5 over Resample by + 18.1 +18.1 pp (CI [ + 13.3 , + 22.9 ] [+13.3,+22.9] ). Its difference from Other-Episode Feedback is smaller, at + 2.3 +2.3 pp (CI [ − 1.1 , + 5.6 ] [-1.1,+5.6] ), with no detected advantage over this same-task feedback control (Figure 4 ; Appendix C.3 ).

The recovery advantage persists in most additional evaluations of API variants, pose noise, and generation seeds. At temperature 0.2 on lifting with pose shift, however, Compiled’s recovery is 19.6 pp lower than Resample’s.
With Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Compiled and Resample solve the same 52 of 55 initial stack failures (94.5% recovery@5). This high recovery rate leaves limited room for further improvement.

On nut insertion, the required rim grasp conflicts with the center-grasp instruction in the pick-and-place template for failed_grasp . Recovery@5 is 82.5% with Compiled and 97.5% with Resample, a difference of − 15.0 -15.0 pp (CI [ − 27.5 , − 2.5 ] [-27.5,-2.5] ). The decrease is consistent with the incompatible grasp instruction, while attempt validity remains similar. Guidance that helps within one task family can therefore be harmful in another.

Our results suggest that reusable task guidance explains the recovery advantage of template-based feedback over resampling in the tested tasks. Fixed guidance and feedback from other failures yield similar recovery point estimates to Compiled, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. Static-from-Start also achieves similar observed overall success to Compiled while using fewer tokens per solved episode. Evaluations should test fixed guidance from the first attempt alongside feedback selected after failure. The Static-from-Start comparison changes both guidance and the generation instruction, so their individual contributions remain unresolved.

Evaluations of self-repair should therefore distinguish the contributions of additional sampling, reusable guidance, and failure-specific information. Resampling provides a baseline for additional sampling, with retry and token budgets matched across methods. Static guidance tests whether instructions are useful before a failure occurs, while mismatched feedback tests the value of matching the coarse failure label to the current episode. These comparisons should check for instructions that conflict with a task’s requirements, such as center-grasp guidance on a task requiring a rim grasp.

Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, static guidance from the first attempt, and previous-program editing, with retry and token budgets matched across methods.

Our findings are limited to simulated manipulation with privileged state and coarse feedback. Some comparisons combine instruction and information changes. Future work should isolate these effects and examine larger models on harder tasks or under tighter budgets. Extending evaluation to visual feedback and physical recovery, including post-failure states and action costs, would clarify when adaptive feedback improves on static guidance.

passages.section: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.location: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.text: We evaluate text-only code generation with privileged state in robosuite 1.5.2 and MuJoCo 3.3.5 using a simulated Panda arm. Python programs run through a documented position-control API in isolated subprocesses with a 60 s timeout. The primitive API includes lift and place_on ; the position-only API omits them. The tasks are cube lifting, stacking, cube-to-zone, and place-in-bin, with additional evaluations on nut insertion and door opening.

passages.location: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.text: The evaluation sets, retry instructions, and outcome measures are summarized in Table A1 . The primary dataset contains 360 Qwen2.5-Coder-7B programs (18.9% initial success). Its 292 failures unrelated to infrastructure errors are divided into 40 development and 252 evaluation failures by initial-program hash.

passages.section: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.location: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.text: After an initial failure, each condition receives at most five retries from the original scene. Within a study, conditions share the model, task, API, decoding settings, and retry cap. Unless stated otherwise, generation uses temperature 0.7, top- p p 0.95, a 1,024-token completion limit, and a 768-whitespace-token feedback cap. Reflection calls allow 256 completion tokens.

passages.section: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.location: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.text: Conditional recovery@ k k is the fraction of initial failures solved within k k sequential retries. Task success is checked by an independent final-state geometric predicate. Valid programs compile, call only documented functions, and finish before timeout. An execution counts as a safety violation if it leaves an object off the table.

passages.section: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.location: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.text: Confidence intervals for paired differences use 10,000 bootstrap replicates. Exact McNemar tests assess significance at the final retry, with Holm correction within each predefined comparison group. Intervals are 95% unless an earlier secondary result is marked 90%. The primary analysis treats each stored initial failure as one observation. An exploratory bootstrap over the 159 task–API–scene clusters accounts for dependence within scene configurations and retains the + 17.1 +17.1 pp Compiled–Resample difference (95% CI [ + 10.1 , + 24.2 ] [+10.1,+24.2] ).

passages.section: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.location: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.text: Fixed-token analyses replay logged calls in order. Each call’s prompt and maximum completion allowance must fit within the remaining budget. Token use includes prompts, completions, and reflection calls. The budgets are 2,000, 5,000, and 9,500 tokens. No call fits within the original 1,000-token budget. In end-to-end studies, tokens per solved episode is total token use across all scenes, including attempt 0 and unsolved scenes, divided by the number of solved episodes.

Development and evaluation contain distinct initial programs but share 24 of the 159 evaluation scene configurations. The earliest core comparisons pair stored initial failures, though a placement-sampler seeding limitation allowed retry layouts to differ. Later studies seed every reset, and the subsequent evaluation with the original generation instruction uses rebuilt software. Each comparison uses a single software build. Seeding does not guarantee bitwise deterministic simulation.

The generalization question was revised after the core results, with settings and analysis fixed before generation for that study. The Static-from-Start study was also specified before generation. Fixed Task Template was selected on development data, so its first held-out comparison is exploratory. Later studies reused this fixed text. Direct+Compiled was selected in a separate 116-failure pilot.
Failure labels were audited on scripted faults, without human audits of natural failures. Oracle-hint performance and template-authoring cost were not measured.

passages.location: B.1 Failure labels and template selection
passages.text: The labeler checks execution errors, safety events, absence of API calls, and task subgoals in a fixed priority order to assign one of 14 failure labels. The lookup Compile ​ ( 𝑙𝑎𝑏𝑒𝑙 , 𝑣𝑎𝑟𝑖𝑎𝑛𝑡 ) \textsc{Compile}(\mathit{label},\mathit{variant}) returns a diagnosis and MUST/NEVER instructions. Three templates vary across APIs, yielding 17 label-specific texts. All templates, API substitutions, and the generic fallback are reproduced in Appendix D .

passages.section: B.1 Failure labels and template selection
passages.location: B.1 Failure labels and template selection
passages.text: Compiled adds one feedback record after each failure. Records are ordered newest first, with duplicate instruction lines removed and the shared feedback-length limit applied. Attempt indices remain in the headers, so repeated labels can appear under different attempt headers.

Regeneration with Compiled, mismatched feedback, and fixed guidance is described in Algorithm 1 , with selection rules in Appendix B.3 . Each failure record includes its label and the information used to match source episodes.
Algorithm 1 Reset-and-retry regeneration with condition-specific feedback
Regeneration prompts omit the previous program (Table A2 ). Direct+Compiled and Reflection Repair include it and request a revision, changing both code exposure and the generation instruction.
Table A2: Prompt inputs for each feedback and editing condition. Source-episode selection and prompt construction are specified below.

Condition Feedback supplied to program generation Resample / Compiled No feedback / accumulated templates for the observed labels. Other-Episode Feedback Accumulated feedback from a matched source episode. Different-Label Feedback Feedback from another failure, prioritizing a different label. Permuted Labels A fixed permutation replaces every observed label with a different label. Cross-Task Feedback A fixed assignment of source episodes from a different task. Fixed Task Template One fixed development-selected template per task, reused after failure. Static-from-Start The complete Fixed Task Template retry prompt from attempt 0 onward. Initial-Label Only The initial failure’s template, unchanged across retries. All-Template Union Goal-compatible templates ordered by development frequency. Static Prior One fixed task-independent text per model, without accumulation. Placebo / Repeated API Rules Length-matched generic instructions / existing API execution rules. Direct+Compiled Previous program and accumulated feedback templates. Reflection Accumulated model-written critiques; previous program hidden. Reflection Repair Previous program, latest critique, and truncated execution log.

Other-Episode Feedback selects feedback from another episode matched by task, API variant, and initial task-progress bin. Progress is the fraction of ordered subgoals completed before the first unmet subgoal, grouped into four equal-width bins over [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Source histories are limited to the evaluated episode’s failure count.

Different-Label Feedback selects one source record per observed label from the same task, preferring a different label in the same progress bin. If none is available, the progress-bin match is relaxed before allowing the same label; the task match is always retained. In the primary evaluation, all 627 selected records had a different failure label from the corresponding observed failure. Both controls use Compiled’s feedback ordering, deduplication, and length limit.

Fixed Task Template uses the most frequent failure label with task-compatible guidance for each task, selected from the fixed 40-failure development set. Static-from-Start also reuses the retry instruction and historical failure header (Appendix C.2 ).
Following Reflexion [ 2 ] , Reflection uses a separate critic call that receives the previous program and truncated log. Generation receives only the accumulated critique.
A generation prompt concatenates four blocks:
API documentation → \rightarrow task and objects → \rightarrow condition-specific feedback → \rightarrow generation instruction .

passages.text: The earlier end-to-end study uses 700 separate scenes and the original generation instruction. Attempt 0 succeeds on 147 scenes, leaving 553 shared failures. Compiled reaches 92.9% overall success, compared with 73.1% for Resample and 95.6% for Fixed Task Template. The template comparison is exploratory.

Across the seven eligible Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B settings, Compiled improves recovery over Resample by + 18.1 +18.1 pp (95% CI [ + 13.3 , + 22.9 ] [+13.3,+22.9] ). Its difference from Other-Episode Feedback is smaller, at + 2.3 +2.3 pp ( [ − 1.1 , + 5.6 ] [-1.1,+5.6] ). The additional studies below are excluded from this combined estimate.

Recovery gains vary across API and perturbation settings. With the position-only API, Compiled improves recovery over Resample by + 30.0 +30.0 pp on cube-to-zone. Both methods reach 93.3% recovery on place-in-bin. Across three generation seeds, Compiled exceeds Resample in all six tested seed–setting pairs ( + 10.7 +10.7 to + 26.7 +26.7 pp). With 5 mm pose noise, the difference is + 16.7 +16.7 pp on lift and + 10.0 +10.0 pp on stack, with only the lift interval excluding zero. At temperature 0.2 on lift with pose shift, Compiled’s recovery is 19.6 19.6 pp lower than Resample’s (90% CI [ − 28.6 , − 10.7 ] [-28.6,-10.7] ).

The model-specific results cover different levels of initial success (Figure A2 ). DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B falls below the minimum initial-success rate required for inclusion on both tasks. Its combined recovery is 50.8% for Compiled and 41.7% for Resample ( n = 120 n{=}120 ; difference + 9.2 +9.2 pp, [ − 1.7 , + 20.0 ] [-1.7,+20.0] ). The separate door-opening study has 1.3% initial success and also falls below the minimum required for inclusion.

With Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, all 80 lift scenes succeed initially. On stack, 105 of 160 initial attempts succeed, and Compiled and Resample solve the same 52 of the remaining 55 failures (94.5%). The paired interval has zero width because the methods produce identical outcomes on these 55 failures. Equivalence on other evaluation sets remains untested.
Figure A2: Recovery differences between Compiled and Resample across model-specific studies. Each point compares Compiled with Resample within a separately evaluated model and task set.

On nut insertion, Compiled recovers 82.5% of initial failures, compared with 97.5% for Resample ( n = 40 n{=}40 ; − 15.0 -15.0 pp, 95% CI [ − 27.5 , − 2.5 ] [-27.5,-2.5] ). The decrease is consistent with the center-grasp instruction conflicting with the required rim grasp. Other-Episode Feedback reaches 62.5% recovery. Attempt validity remains similar for Compiled and Resample (85.1% and 84.9%).
